newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Death toll in Brazilian air crash is lowered to 98.
newsitem.headline: Death toll in Brazilian air crash is lowered to 98.

text.p: The death toll from a plane crash in the Brazilian city of Sao Paulo was lowered on Sunday to 98 people after confusion over four bodies was cleared up, a spokeswoman for the city morgue said.
The crash occurred on Thursday when a Fokker-100 aircraft from Brazil's TAM airline plowed into a densely populated area minutes after takeoff from Congonhas airport.
All 96 passengers and crew members on the shuttle flight to Rio de Janeiro died, and it had been thought that six people on the ground were also killed.
But officials at the city morgue have now revised the death toll down to 98 from 102.

"We were notified early Friday morning of the imminent arrival of four more bodies. They did not arrive here, however, and the director of the morgue is satisfied they were not involved in the crash," the spokeswoman said.
The severe burning of many of the bodies has meant that only 85 have been identified so far.
Lengthy DNA tests may now have to be used, but morgue officials will continue to try to use other methods until Monday afternoon, the spokeswoman said.
TAM officials have declined to comment on the cause of the crash other than to say that the plane lacked power.
Witnesses at the airport say they saw the thrust reverser on the Fokker's right turbine deploy automatically as the plane raced down the runway.
The thrust reverser, used during landings to help bring a plane to a stop, reverses the direction of an engine's thrust, creating aerodynamic resistance.
Many of the passengers on the early morning shuttle were businessmen, and the country's financial community has sharply felt the loss of a large number of well-known banking and business executives.

Citibank, Bank of Boston, Siemens and Coca-Cola were among the multinational companies that had executives on board. Unibanco, Brazil's second-largest financial institution, lost eight of its executives.
